meta.title: GCL Programming Language
meta.subtitle: A C-based, education-focused language designed for GnuchanOS.

sections.title: What is GCL?
paragraphs: GCL is a C-based programming language at the center of the GnuchanOS project. Its goal is to provide a simple and readable syntax for both education and game development.
It is written in small .c files, making the source easy to read and understand.
The book has three tracks: GCL, Lua and Python. Each track starts from zero and ends with a runnable raylib project; the Lua and Python tracks are driven from GCL through the Embed module.

notes.text: GCL is very close to C. If you know C, learning GCL takes a few hours.

sections.title: First Program
paragraphs: The simplest GCL program contains a main function and uses printf for output.
Note: GCL uses {} placeholders instead of C's %s / %d. Formatting supports syntax like {.2f}.
printf / scanf are built-in; you may also use the prefixed forms Stdio.printf / Stdio.scanf by declaring #native .

sections.title: Running
paragraphs: Save GCL files with the .gcsf extension. Then you can run them with:

code.src:
gcl -run file.gcsf
# Debug mode:
gcl -debug -run file.gcsf

sections.title: Vanilla C Types
paragraphs: GCL supports C's standard types: char, short, int, float, double, long int, long long int, long double and unsigned int.

sections.title: GCL Specific Types
paragraphs: GCL also provides its own fixed-bit-width and UTF-8-supporting types:

sections.title: Variable Declaration
paragraphs: Variables are declared as type name = value;. Multiple variables can be separated by commas.

notes.text: gcChar stores the real length for UTF-8 strings; it is not limited like C's strlen.

sections.title: Arithmetic and Assignment
paragraphs: Basic arithmetic operators are the same as C: + - / * %. Assignments can use += -= *= /=.

sections.title: Bitwise Operators
paragraphs: Bit-level operations: & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ~ (NOT), << (left shift), >> (right shift).

code.src:
int a = 0b1100;  // 12
int b = 0b1010;  // 10
int and_ = a & b; // 0b1000 = 8
int or_ = a | b;  // 0b1110 = 14
int xor_ = a ^ b; // 0b0110 = 6
int not_ = ~a;    // bitwise NOT
int left = a << 2; // 48
int right = a >> 2; // 3

sections.title: Comparison and Logic
paragraphs: Comparison: == != < > <= >=. Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT).
Note: => syntax is also supported as >=.

sections.title: sizeof / strlen
paragraphs: sizeof() and strlen() functions are supported; sizeof()/sizeof() can compute array size.

sections.title: if / else if / else
paragraphs: Standard conditional statements are the same as C.

sections.title: switch / case
paragraphs: switch, case, default and break are supported.

sections.title: for
paragraphs: C-style for (init; condition; increment) loops are supported.

sections.title: while
paragraphs: while (condition) loops are supported.

sections.title: Function Declaration
paragraphs: Functions are declared like in C. Return type, name and parameters are specified.

sections.title: Scope
paragraphs: The global keyword makes a variable usable in a wider scope, while inline declares a local variable.

sections.title: const, public / private
paragraphs: const makes a value immutable. public variables are accessible from other files, while private is only valid in its scope.

sections.title: struct
paragraphs: struct can group data of different types together.

sections.title: typedef struct
paragraphs: typedef allows defining named structs. Here is the full struct example from simple_doc.md — it covers: empty struct + dot-assign, positional brace initializer, designated (.member = value) initializer, partial initializer, variable-based initializer, struct copy, empty + fill, and a struct returned from a function.
sections.output:
A: GNUCHANOS
B: ALPHA
C: BETA
D: GAMMA
E: DELTA
F: DELTA
G: EPSILON
H: ZETA
Number: 70

sections.title: enum
paragraphs: enum defines named constant integer values. It can be used both anonymous and with typedef.

sections.title: #define and #undef
paragraphs: #define defines constants and macros. Function-like macros are also supported.

sections.title: #if / #ifdef / #ifndef / #elif / #else / #endif
paragraphs: Preprocessor conditionals are supported. #if expressions evaluate arithmetic, comparison and logical operators; the defined() operator also works.

notes.text: #if expressions support both defined(X) and defined X forms.

sections.title: #warning / #error / #debug
paragraphs: Colored diagnostic messages are shown with #warning (yellow), #error (red) and #debug (blue).

code.src:
#warning This is a warning
#debug This is a debug message
#error This is an error message

sections.title: #native
paragraphs: The #native directive loads a module from .dll or .so files in the Library/ directory.

sections.title: How a native module is found
paragraphs: #native loads Name.dll (Windows) or Name.so (Linux). The runtime searches in this order: the executable's own Library/ directory, base_dir/Library/, Library/ in the working directory, then the system search path. The first hit wins.

A module exports exactly one symbol, gcl__get_functions (the name lowercased), which returns a table of { name, fn } entries. Every member receives its arguments as an array of strings and returns a single double — the module ABI is text in, one value out.

Because a module only sees strings, a value that cannot be expressed as text travels through a module-side slot instead: a call writes the struct into a scratch global and separate read-back members (Last*) publish its components. Handles work the same way — an image, font or sound is returned as an integer index into the module's registry.

sections.title: Callbacks — letting C call back into GCL
paragraphs: Some raylib members take a C function pointer: SetTraceLogCallback, the four SetLoadFile*Callback / SetSaveFile*Callback members, SetAudioStreamCallback and the Attach*Processor pair. A GCL function cannot be passed as a C pointer, so these members take the name of a GCL function, and the module resolves it through a host table the runtime hands it when the module is loaded.

That host table (GclHostApi) is optional and versioned: a module that does not export gcl_module_set_host behaves exactly as before, so the ABI stays backward compatible. Arguments are typed — text or number — because GCL binds a parameter as a string only when it is actually given a string.

Thread safety is the interesting part. The interpreter's environment is shared state, so it may only be touched from the main thread. The trace log and file callbacks are invoked by raylib on the calling thread, so they call GCL directly. The audio callback runs on its own thread and never enters GCL: it only pops samples from a lock-free ring buffer, while the main thread produces them inside gcl_module_tick, which the runtime runs before every native module call — once per frame in a game loop. An empty buffer yields silence instead of a glitch.

notes.text: Audio works the same way in reverse: the generator is called with the number of frames to produce and pushes samples with AudioPush(v); AudioQueued() reports the current buffer level.

File callbacks move bytes through a module-side buffer: a read callback pushes bytes with FileDataPush(v) and the module hands raylib a copy; a write callback exposes the incoming bytes with FileDataAt(i).

sections.title: #extern + #register
paragraphs: #extern loads an external DLL and #register registers C functions.

sections.title: #include
paragraphs: #include includes another GCL file.

sections.title: Loading and Core Window
paragraphs: The Raylib module is loaded with #native . It provides window, drawing, input and shape functions based on the raylib C library.
All colors are available as constants (e.g. Raylib.RED) encoded as 32-bit packed integers.

sections.title: Drawing
paragraphs: Core drawing functions: BeginDrawing / EndDrawing wrap the frame; ClearBackground, DrawRectangle, DrawCircle, DrawLine, DrawPixel, DrawText, DrawFPS and DrawRectangleLines are available.

sections.title: Input
paragraphs: Keyboard and mouse input functions return 1/0 for states.

sections.title: Shapes
paragraphs: Raylib.Rectangle(x, y, w, h) creates a rectangle value used by raygui widgets.

sections.title: Color Constants
paragraphs: All standard raylib colors are available as 32-bit packed integers.

sections.title: Loading and Core GUI
paragraphs: The Raygui module is loaded with #native . It must be used together with #native ; widgets read the last Raylib.Rectangle as their layout rectangle.

sections.title: Widgets
paragraphs: Available raygui widgets. Colored values are passed as 32-bit packed integers.

sections.title: Example: Button and Slider
paragraphs: A small window with a button and a slider. The button click resets a counter; the slider controls a rectangle width.

sections.title: Core Functions
paragraphs: The Math module is loaded with #native .

sections.title: printf / scanf
paragraphs: printf provides output and scanf provides safe input. They are built-in; the prefixed forms Stdio.printf / Stdio.scanf also work when #native is declared. Input is safer than C's scanf — no & or format scanner needed.

sections.title: File Operations
paragraphs: File functions support named arguments: file= and text=.

sections.title: Python and Lua Runtime
paragraphs: The Embed module starts, stops Python and Lua runtimes and provides variable sharing.

sections.title: Methods
paragraphs: Available methods and return values:

notes.text: The variable on the Python/Lua side must be defined in __main__ globals. Sent values are currently int, float, char and soon gcChar.

sections.title: New Project
paragraphs: The gcl -new project_name command creates a new project skeleton.

code.src:
gcl -new Demo

Demo/
    assets/       # automatically visible for raylib
    external/     # .so, .dll files (searched by gcl, python and lua)
    include/      # .gcsf files found by #include
    lib/          # configured by gcl_lib_path
    out/          # Demo, Demo.gcBundle
    scripts/      # main.lua / main.py
    main.gcsf
    project.gcdata

notes.text: The skeleton always contains main.gcsf and project.gcdata. Depending on the Lua/Python switches it also writes scripts/main.lua and/or scripts/main.py, each already a runnable raylib window (Empty, 2D or 3D scene).

sections.title: project.gcdata
paragraphs: Project settings are stored in the project.gcdata JSON file.

code.src:
{
  "project_name": "Demo",
  "developer_name": "developer",
  "version": 0.100,
  "icon": "assets/icon.png",
  "open_lua": true,
  "open_lua_raylib": true,
  "open_python": true,
  "open_python_raylib": true,
  "single_bundle": false,
  "lua_main_file": "main.lua",
  "python_main_file": "main.py",
  "gcl_include_path": "include",
  "gcl_lib_path": "lib",
  "gcl_external_path": "external",
  "python_import_path": "scripts",
  "lua_import_path": "scripts",
  "raylib_asset_directory_path": "assets"
}

sections.title: Build
paragraphs: Project compile and package commands:

code.src:
# Run a single file:
gcl -run file.gcsf

# Run Python / Lua:
gcl -pyrun file.py
gcl -luarun file.lua

# Start IDE:
gcl -ide

# Build project:
gcl -build project.gcdata -o path/dir
#    -> Demo.exe / Demo.gcBundle

sections.title: The Big Picture
paragraphs: GCL is not a compiler. It is a tree-walking interpreter written in C: a .gcsf file is read, transformed and executed inside the same process, and output appears immediately.

Every run travels through four stages — preprocess → lex → parse → run — glued together by one function: gcl_simple_run_source() in language/_SRC/GCL/SimpleRunner/gcl_simple_runner.c. That file is the spine of the language; every other file is a specialist module hanging off it.

The design rule of the whole project is: many small .c files instead of one big file. The lexer knows nothing about the parser, the parser knows nothing about the runner, and the runner never opens a file by itself.

rows: Collects #native, #extern, #register lines before anything else runs
Turns text into a flat token list
Walks the AST, holds variables, loads modules, calls native code

sections.title: Stage 0 — Directives Are Collected First
paragraphs: Before a single macro is expanded, three small scanners walk the raw source line by line and collect the directives that describe the outside world:
collect_native() gathers every #native into a module name list, collect_extern() gathers every #extern , and collect_register() records each #register signature as a compact ret|name|params string.
They run first on purpose: the module list is needed before the program is executed, and the preprocessor would otherwise comment away or expand the very lines that declare the modules.

notes.text: Limits are compile-time constants: at most 32 native modules, 16 extern DLLs, 64 registered functions, 256 macros, 32 include directories.

sections.title: Stage 1 — The Preprocessor
paragraphs: The preprocessor is a line-oriented text transformer, not a full C preprocessor. It walks the source line by line, keeps a macro table and a conditional stack, and writes an expanded buffer that the lexer will read.

Normal lines go through pp_expand_line(), which expands object-like macros and function-like macros — while deliberately skipping anything inside a string literal, so printf("PI") never becomes the value of PI.

notes.text: Function-like macro arguments are split on commas at bracket depth 0, so max(a, f(x, y)) is split correctly into two arguments.

sections.title: Stage 1b — #include Resolution
paragraphs: #include accepts both and "file.gcsf". The file name is resolved against a search path that is prepared once, in pp_init(), from the directory of the running file.
Both / and \ separators are tried, so a project built on Windows and opened on Linux resolves the same include.

code.src:
<base_dir>        # the folder of the running .gcsf file
<base_dir>/include # project include folder
<base_dir>/lib     # project lib folder

sections.title: Stage 1c — #if / #ifdef and Colored Diagnostics
paragraphs: Conditional compilation uses a small Pratt expression evaluator (cond_parse_expr) that understands the full operator precedence ladder: ||, &&, == !=, < > <= >=, + -, * / %, unary ! - + ~ and defined(X) / defined X.

A macro whose value is not a pure number is treated as defined and evaluates to 1; an undefined identifier evaluates to 0. Frames track both whether a branch is active and whether any earlier branch was already taken, so #elif chains behave exactly like C.

rows: Removes the macro from the table

notes.text: Colors are produced with SetConsoleTextAttribute on Windows and ANSI escape codes on POSIX. Diagnostics are suppressed inside an inactive #if branch.

GCL also has its own multi-line comment: #| ... |#. The preprocessor skips it before deciding whether a line is a directive, so documentation blocks that mention a directive are never mistaken for one.

sections.title: Stage 2 — The Lexer
paragraphs: The lexer (gcl_lex) is a single while loop with a position, a line and a column counter. It produces a growable array of GclToken. Crucially, each token stores a pointer into the source plus a length — the text is never copied, which is why the expanded buffer must stay alive until the program has finished running.

Identifiers are classified in two steps: first against the keyword table, then against the type-name table. That is why int and gcChar arrive at the parser as TOK_TYPE_NAME rather than as ordinary identifiers.

rows: if else while for switch case default break continue return struct enum typedef const public private global local inline sizeof strlen true false null try catch finally throw raise defer
int8 int16 int32 int64 int128 uint8..uint128 float16..float128 char short int long float double unsigned void bool gcChar
Double and single quotes, with \ escape awareness
=> is lexed as the same token as >=
Any line starting with # becomes one TOK_PREPROC token

notes.text: Comments are consumed and discarded: // to end of line, /* ... */ blocks, and the GCL-native #| ... |# block.
An unknown character is a hard lexer error — unexpected character at line:col. The token list is discarded and nothing is executed.

sections.title: Stage 3 — The Parser and the AST
paragraphs: The parser is a recursive-descent parser. Its whole vocabulary is two types from gcl_parser.h: GclStmt for statements and GclExpr for expressions. A program is simply an array of statements — there is no separate bytecode form.

Because the AST is the public contract between the parser and the runner, the two halves of the language can be developed and tested independently. That is exactly what language/tests/parser/test_parser.c does.

rows: — error handling and defer add no expression kind

notes.text: AST_EXPR_INIT_LIST is what makes brace initialisation work — Hello b = { 20, 30.5, "world", "ALPHA" } arrives as one init-list node and is filled in by the runner.

sections.title: Stage 4 — The Runner
paragraphs: The runner (gcl_run_program in gcl_runner.c) is a classic recursive tree walker. It owns a GclEnv — the environment — and a Runner cursor carrying control-flow flags: return_flag, return_value, break_flag, continue_flag.

Execution happens in two passes. The first pass walks the top level and executes only declarations — functions, typedefs, enums and structs. The second pass executes everything else. This is why a function may be called on line 1 even though it is defined on line 40.

notes.text: main() is not magic syntax — the runner simply looks it up with find_func(&env, "main") after the top level has run. If it is missing, the program still succeeds; only its top-level statements execute.

sections.title: The Variable Environment
paragraphs: A variable is a Var node in a singly linked list. Each node can hold a number, a string, a fixed-size numeric array, an array of strings, an array of structs, or an inline struct value — all in one struct. The decl_type field remembers what the variable was declared as, which is what enables clamping and cross-language marshalling later.
Lookup is a linear scan. For an educational language with small programs this is deliberate: it keeps the data structure readable, and the code that operates on it obvious.

notes.text: Every numeric value in GCL is a double at runtime. Integer behaviour is produced by truncate_to_declared_type() at assignment time, not by separate integer storage.

sections.title: Types, Clamping and Truncation
paragraphs: Because storage is a double, GCL emulates the fixed-width types at the boundary. Whenever a value is written to a variable, truncate_to_declared_type(val, decl_type) converts it according to the declared type: integers are rounded, uint8 wraps into 0..255, int8 into -128..127, int16/uint16 and the int32 family follow the same rule, and the float32 family is rounded to single precision.
gcChar is the exception on purpose: it keeps a real UTF-8 string, so strlen is not the way to measure it.

rows: Single character; marshalled to native modules as a one-character string
Wrapped into the corresponding bit-width range

sections.title: Structs, Enums and Typedefs
paragraphs: Three registries live in the environment: TypedefDef (alias → base type), StructDef (member names + member types) and EnumDef (constant names). They are filled in pass one, so a struct can be used by a function defined above it.

A struct value is a linked list of GclStructValue nodes — each node holds a name, a numeric value or a string, the member's declared type (so clamping still applies per field), and optionally a nested member list. Because clone_struct_members() exists, Hello f = e; performs a real copy instead of aliasing.

notes.text: All four initialisation styles from the language guide — positional braces, designated .member = value, partial, and variable-based — are filled by the same helper: fill_members_from_init_list().

sections.title: Functions, Scope and main()
paragraphs: User functions are stored as FuncDef nodes holding a name, a parameter name list and a pointer to the body statement. Calling one copies the current Runner, binds the parameters as environment variables, executes the body block, then reads return_value and clears the control-flow flags.
global and inline change where a variable is written. Block-scoped variables (for example a for init variable) are removed from the environment when their block ends, using env_remove_var().

notes.text: argc is bound as a number and argv reads from env->arg_vals, which the CLI fills from gcl -run file.gcsf a1 a2.

sections.title: Native Modules — #native
paragraphs: #native does not link anything at compile time. At run time native_load() searches for a shared library and opens it with LoadLibraryA (Windows) or dlopen (Linux).
The search order is fixed and tries the most specific location first, which is what allows the same source to run from the build tree, from a project folder, or from a built bundle.

code.src:
1. <exe_dir>/Library/<Name>.dll        # next to gcl.exe (the normal case)
2. <base_dir>/Library/<Name>.dll       # the folder of the running .gcsf
3. Library/<Name>.dll                  # relative to the working directory
4. <Name>.dll                          # whatever the OS loader can find

notes.text: A module exports exactly one symbol: gcl__get_functions(int *count), lowercased. It returns a table of { name, function pointer } entries — the interface in include/gcl_module.h.

Every argument crossing the boundary is serialised to a string. That is why a native function signature is double f(int argc, const char **argv) — numbers are parsed with atof inside the module, strings are used directly.

sections.title: The Struct → Native Bridge
paragraphs: Passing a struct to a native function is the most interesting piece of marshalling in GCL. flatten_struct_members() walks the struct value in declaration order and appends every member as a separate string argument.

This is what makes raylib work: Camera3D camera; Raylib.BeginMode3D(camera); becomes eleven string arguments — position.x, position.y, position.z, target.x ... fovy, projection — exactly the flattened C struct raylib expects. Taking the address of a struct (&camera) flattens it the same way.

sections.title: #extern and #register — Arbitrary DLLs
paragraphs: #extern loads a library that was not written for GCL, and #register teaches the runner the type of each parameter so it can marshal values correctly.

The parser turns a registration line into a compact string — ret|name|params — and extern_register_parse() converts it into a GclExternReg record with a return type and up to eight parameter types. At call time call_extern_func() resolves the symbol with GetProcAddress/dlsym and builds the call from those types.

notes.text: A maximum of eight parameters is remembered per registered function. Registering more than eight will silently ignore the extras — wrap such a call in a GCL function instead.

sections.title: The {} Format Engine and Safe Input
paragraphs: GCL has no %s / %d. Its formatter lives in the Stdio module: fn_printf scans the format string character by character and, on every {}, prints the next argument as-is. {.2f} switches that argument to fixed-point output.
Because printf is also available unqualified, the runner resolves a bare printf(...) by lazily loading the built-in Stdio module — the same code path as Stdio.printf(...).

notes.text: scanf is intentionally not scanf: the runner's do_scanf() reads a whole line, parses it according to the target variable's declared type and writes it into the environment. There is no &, no format specifier and no buffer-overflow surface.
The completion engine can warn about this at edit time: it compares the number of {} placeholders with the number of arguments (see the Diagnostics section of the IDE chapter).

sections.title: Cross-Process Variables — the Shared Store
paragraphs: Lua and Python run in separate processes (see the Embed chapter), so they cannot share GCL's memory. gcl_shared_state.h bridges them with a real memory-mapped file: a fixed array of 64 slots, each holding a key and a value, guarded by a spinlock.

Every process maps the same file — the path comes from the GCL_SHARED_FILE environment variable — and a single read or write is one memory access plus a very short critical section. This is what makes a shared variable in a game loop fast enough to be usable every frame.

notes.text: The store is bounded: 64 keys, key length 64, value length 128. Values are stored as text and converted with atof on the way out.

An earlier version rewrote a whole file and renamed it on every set — producing disk lag and a "teleport" effect when two processes overwrote each other with stale snapshots. The mapped-memory version was the fix.

sections.title: Debug Mode and Debug Gates
paragraphs: gcl -debug -run file.gcsf sets a single global flag, gcl_debug. Every internal trace line goes through one gate function, gcl_debugf(), which returns immediately when the flag is off.
That single gate is what keeps a normal run clean while still allowing step-by-step tracing when something goes wrong.

code.src:
gcl -run app.gcsf          # normal: silent internals
gcl -debug -run app.gcsf    # prints gcl_run_program: start / return 0 and module traces

sections.title: Terminal Programs — #pragma commandline
paragraphs: The IDE is a GUI application and starts child processes without a console, so a program that waits for input would hang. #pragma commandline solves this: when the pragma is present, gcl_terminal_enter() re-launches the program in its own terminal window.

On Windows the re-launch goes through cmd /k, so the window stays open after the program ends and the output remains readable. On POSIX a terminal emulator is located (respecting GCL_TERMINAL_CMD) and the program is started inside it. The GCL_TERMINAL=1 marker is inherited by child processes, so Embed.Run(type="lua") opens a separate terminal of its own.

notes.text: All three spellings are accepted: commandline, cmdline and the historical commendline. Pragmas written inside a #| ... |# documentation block are ignored.

sections.title: Memory Model and Ownership Rules
paragraphs: There is no garbage collector. Ownership is explicit and follows three rules that run through the whole codebase: whoever allocates, frees; token lexemes point into the source, so the source must outlive the token list; and the environment frees everything at exit through env_cleanup().

The second rule is the one that bites. gcl_simple_run_source() therefore keeps the preprocessed buffer allocated until gcl_run_program() has fully returned, and frees tokens and the AST only afterwards.

code.src:
processed = pp_process(pp, src);      // owns the text
free(pp table);                        // macros are no longer needed

tokens = gcl_lex(processed, ...);       // tokens POINT INTO processed
prog   = gcl_parse(tokens, ...);        // AST owns its own strings

rc = gcl_run_program(prog, ...);        // processed must still be alive

gcl_program_free(prog);
gcl_token_free(tokens);
free(processed);                        // freed LAST

notes.text: The bundle runner shares this rule from the other side: a blob read out of a .gcBundle is not null-terminated, so it is copied into a terminated buffer before lexing. Reading it directly used to produce random-data lexer errors.

sections.title: The IDE Is a Plugin, Not a Program
paragraphs: The IDE is not part of gcl.exe. It is built as a separate shared library — Programs/ide.dll on Windows, Programs/ide.so on Linux — and gcl.exe loads it on demand.

run_ide() in gcl_main.c finds its own directory, builds the path /Programs/ide.dll, opens it with LoadLibraryA / dlopen and resolves one symbol: gcl_ide_run. That single entry point takes the path the IDE should open and returns an exit code.
The split exists for a practical reason: the IDE pulls in raylib, the whole completion engine and the build sources, while gcl.exe must stay small enough to be copied as the base of every built game.

notes.text: Before loading the IDE, gcl.exe exports its own path through the GCL_EXE_PATH environment variable. The IDE cannot see argv, so this is how it later runs gcl -run and copies itself as a build output.
If Programs/ide.dll is missing, the build did not include the IDE sources. The CLI prints a clear message instead of failing silently.

sections.title: Launching the IDE
paragraphs: gcl_ide_run(path) accepts three kinds of argument, and the workspace root (called ed.cwd) is decided from it.
This matters more than it looks: the explorer tree is built from ed.cwd, so getting it wrong makes the IDE show the wrong folder even though the right file is open.

rows: Explorer shows the project, no tabs open
File opens as a tab and the explorer shows its project

notes.text: For a file argument the parent directory is derived with fs_parent_dir(). A bare file name yields an empty string, which falls back to the working directory.

sections.title: Window, Frame Loop and the Font
paragraphs: The IDE opens a raylib window of 1200 × 760, makes it resizable, pins the frame rate to 60 FPS and disables raylib's default ESC-to-exit behaviour (SetExitKey(KEY_NULL)), because ESC is used to dismiss popups and panels.

Text is drawn with GNU FreeFont FreeMono — a monospace font under the SIL OFL 1.1 licence — compiled into the binary as a byte array in embed_freemono.c. Loading from memory rather than from a file path removes an entire class of "font not found" problems: the IDE works no matter where it is started from.

notes.text: Generating the atlas at 48 px and scaling down with a bilinear filter keeps small code readable. Generating it at 16 px and scaling up would produce hard pixel edges.

sections.title: The Buffer — the Unit of Editing
paragraphs: Everything the user types goes into a GclIdeBuffer (ide_buffer.c). A buffer owns its text, its cursor, its scroll offsets, its dirty flag, its file path — and, importantly, its own selection anchor and its own undo/redo history.

Keeping the selection anchor in the buffer rather than in one shared editor field is a deliberate fix: with a single shared anchor, switching tabs leaked a selection across files and Delete could erase the wrong range.

rows: The text itself, with a growable capacity
Insertion point and the other end of the selection
Unsaved changes marker for the title bar and close prompt
The file on disk this buffer is bound to

sections.title: Undo as Edit Groups
paragraphs: Undo is snapshot-based: gcl_ide_buffer_snapshot() pushes a copy of the current text onto the undo stack before a mutation. Used naively that would make pasting a paragraph undo one character at a time.

Edit groups solve this. begin_edit() raises a counter and end_edit() lowers it; inside the group, the first real change takes exactly one snapshot and every following one is suppressed. Replacing a selection, pasting, and auto-indent therefore each undo as a single step. Groups nest correctly.

notes.text: Because the snapshot stores the whole buffer, undo_suspend exists to make the cost proportional to real edits rather than to every intermediate keystroke.

sections.title: Tabs and Split View
paragraphs: The editor supports two independent panes. Pane 0 is the main list (ed->tabs / active_tab); pane 1 owns a second list (split_right_tabs). Each pane has its own tab strip, its own scroll position and its own focused tab.

The pane state helpers (editor_pane_empty, editor_pane_cur, editor_set_split_focus, editor_ensure_valid_split_focus, tab_fold_split_into_main) deliberately contain no drawing code. That is what allows them to be driven by a headless test instead of only being reachable through a running window.

notes.text: last_cursor[] is an array for a reason: with one shared field, moving the caret in one pane made the other pane believe its caret had moved and reset the user's manual scroll position.

sections.title: The Explorer and the Context Menu
paragraphs: The file tree is a flat TreeModel: an array of TreeNode records, each holding a path, an is_dir flag and an indent depth. Expansion state is kept as a list of expanded directory paths (expanded_dirs) rather than as a flag inside the node, so a rescan never loses which folders the user opened.
The tree is rebuilt by tree_rescan(), which is throttled through ed.last_tree_scan so a large project is not re-read on every frame. Only files with supported extensions appear.

rows: Absolute path to the system clipboard
Base name to the system clipboard

notes.text: Copy Path uses fs_absolute_path(); if the system call fails it copies the given path unchanged, so the menu item never produces an empty clipboard.

sections.title: Editing Behaviour
paragraphs: The editor is designed to feel like a normal code editor, which means a number of details that are easy to miss.

Automatic block indentation on Enter is implemented by editor_insert_newline_autoindent(), which knows about GCL and Python blocks. Tab and Shift+Tab call editor_indent_selection(): with a selection they indent or outdent whole lines, without one they insert a tab. Files that use tabs are recognised, and the drawing code shares the same tab-stop arithmetic with the measuring code — if they disagreed, the caret would visibly drift away from the text. Typing a closing bracket when an opener is already there calls editor_handle_bracket_close(), which skips over the existing character instead of inserting a duplicate.

Key repeat is handled by two separate helpers. Arrow-key navigation repeat uses its own timer, while editing keys (Backspace, Delete) use key_repeat_fire() with a short first delay followed by a fast rate. Pressing an arrow key while a selection exists collapses the selection to the nearest edge — VSCode behaviour — so the next Delete removes a predictable range.

sections.title: Syntax Highlighting
paragraphs: Highlighting is line-based and driven by a small tokenizer, gcl_token_type(line, len, start, &tok_len, lang). It classifies the token starting at an offset, and gcl_token_color() maps that class to a color from the active GclIdeTheme.

The keyword list is language-aware: gcl_is_keyword_for(word, lang) lets the same editor highlight GCL, Lua and Python files correctly. The theme carries a separate color for every token class, so switching themes recolors code, comments and the gutter together.

rows: Editor background and the current-line band
Code text and the line-number column

sections.title: The Completion Engine — Architecture
paragraphs: The most substantial subsystem in the IDE is not the editor — it is the completion engine under language/_SRC/complete/. It is written as independent modules with no raylib dependency at all, which is why it can be unit-tested headlessly by language/tests/complete/test_complete.c.

The editor only supplies two things: the buffer text and the cursor offset. Everything else — which suggestions exist, in what order, and whether the popup should appear at all — is decided by the engine.

rows: The facade: gcl_complete_query(), result lifetime, dedup table
What is under the cursor: string, comment, member access, call, preprocessor line
Symbol and type tables extracted from the source
Type inference and member resolving for X. chains
Matching, scoring and choosing the default entry
mtime-based file cache and parse-result cache

notes.text: The engine is deliberately separate from gcl_lsp_scan.c, which is the older, simpler project symbol scanner used as a fallback.

sections.title: Completion — Context, Scope and Type Resolution
paragraphs: The engine answers a query in three steps.

Context (gcl_context_analyze) decides what kind of place the cursor is in and returns a GclContextKind: CTX_NONE, CTX_MEMBER, CTX_IDENT, CTX_CALL_ARGS, CTX_TYPE_DECL, CTX_VALUE_ASSIGN, CTX_PREPROC, CTX_NATIVE_MODULE, CTX_INCLUDE, CTX_EXTERN, CTX_LIB, CTX_REGISTER, CTX_DOC_COMMENT or CTX_STRING_PATH. It also extracts the member chain — up to 16 links — so a.b.c. is understood, not only a..

Scope (complete_scope.c) extracts symbols and user types from the text, tagging each with a scope_rank — 0 local, 1 parameter, 2 global, 3 included file, 4 builtin. Symbol insertion and lookup go through an open-addressed hash table, which is what keeps a 43 KB file responsive: the earlier linear insertion was O(n²) per keystroke.

Type resolution (complete_type.c) turns the chain into members. Raylib.GetMousePosition(). resolves because the native database records the return type Vector2 and the Vector2 struct fields are known. If a chain cannot be resolved, the list stays empty and the popup closes — showing the members of some unrelated struct would be worse than showing nothing.

code.src:
Raylib.              -> all Raylib module members (°)
Raylib.GetMousePosition().  -> Vector2 -> .x / .y
camera.              -> members of the camera variable's declared type
unknownThing.        -> unresolved -> popup CLOSED (never a guessed list)

notes.text: The Raylib. list alone contains around 670 members. Deduplication therefore uses a hash table, not a linear scan — the naive version performed roughly 224,000 string comparisons for a single query.

sections.title: Completion — Native API Database
paragraphs: The Raylib and Raygui completion tables are generated, not hand-written. tools/gen_native_db.py parses Modules/gcl_raylib.c and Modules/gcl_raygui.c and emits complete_native_db.c.

This is a consistency guarantee, not a convenience: because the tables are derived from the bindings that are actually compiled, a function whose binding changed cannot keep suggesting its old signature. The generator is idempotent — it does not rewrite the file when the content is unchanged — so a no-op run does not force the IDE DLL to be rebuilt.

code.src:
python tools/gen_native_db.py
# reads : _SRC/Modules/gcl_raylib.c, _SRC/Modules/gcl_raygui.c
# writes: _SRC/complete/complete_native_db.c
# also  : cross-checks every binding against raylib.h / raygui.h

notes.text: The build runs the generator automatically (ensure_native_db() in makefile.py) before compiling the IDE.

sections.title: Completion — Caching, Ranking and Diagnostics
paragraphs: Re-parsing the buffer on every keystroke is the classic way to make an editor feel slow, so the engine has two caches.

complete_index.c caches file contents together with their modification time, and — more importantly — caches the parsed scope keyed by a hash of the buffer text. Moving the cursor or refreshing the popup does not change the text, so nothing is re-parsed. A separate gcl_index_generation() counter increases only when a file is genuinely re-read, which forces dependent scans to be rebuilt so symbols deleted from a file actually disappear.

complete_rank.c then scores everything: exact match, prefix match, CamelCase acronym (GMP → GetMousePosition), scope proximity, kind priority for the current context, and which file the symbol came from. It sorts, filters and sets best_index — the entry Enter will accept.

complete_diag.c runs independently of the popup: if the cursor is inside a closed printf call it counts the {} placeholders and compares them with the argument count, producing a warning strip when they disagree.

code.src:
exact match      "DrawLine" == "DrawLine"        strongest
prefix           "Draw"     -> "DrawLine"
CamelCase        "GMP"      -> "GetMousePosition"
scope proximity  local > param > global > include > builtin
kind priority    functions get a bonus inside f( )
origin file      symbols from the active file rank higher

notes.text: The popup itself is drawn by ide_complete_ui.c, which is a pure renderer: it draws the list, the documentation panel for the selected item, and the signature strip for the call the cursor is inside. Type icons are drawn as vector glyphs, never emoji.

sections.title: Run — How the IDE Executes a Project
paragraphs: Running a project is not the same as running a file, and the difference is one environment variable.

editor_run_project() locates project.gcdata, derives the project root, checks that main.gcsf exists, warns when a default project folder is missing, and then sets GCL_PROJECT_DIR to the project root and GCL_SHARED_FILE next to it. Only then does it start the process.

That variable is essential: Embed.Run(type="lua") looks for /scripts/main.lua. Without it, the child process would resolve the script against the workspace and open the wrong file. The child process inherits the value, and a standalone gcl -run preserves an externally set value instead of overwriting it.

code.src:
find project.gcdata
base_dir   = parent of project.gcdata
main_gcsf  = <base_dir>/main.gcsf      -> must exist
warn if a default folder is missing

GCL_PROJECT_DIR = <base_dir>
GCL_SHARED_FILE = <base_dir>/gcl_shared.state

cmd = "<GCL_EXE_PATH>" -run "<main_gcsf>" 2>&1
gcl_ide_proc_start(ed, cmd, main_gcsf, logf)

notes.text: A single .gcsf file that is not part of a project is run through the editor's own Run command, which uses the file's directory as base_dir — the same rule as the CLI.

sections.title: The Asynchronous Process Layer
paragraphs: The IDE must never block. Running a child process with a synchronous popen and reading it with fgets freezes the whole window until the program exits, and because the child's handle is never kept, closing the IDE leaves the program running.

ide_proc.c solves both problems. On Windows it uses CreateProcess with anonymous pipes and puts the process in a Job Object, so terminating the job kills the whole process tree — cmd.exe and the gcl.exe it started — in one call. On POSIX it uses fork + exec with a pipe. Output is collected once per frame and appended to both the IDE output panel and the project's project.gclog file.

There is one subtle platform detail worth knowing: on Windows a ReadFile on a pipe blocks when no data is available, which would freeze the IDE anyway. The reader therefore calls PeekNamedPipe first and only reads when bytes are actually waiting.

notes.text: The redirection 2>&1 in the command line is what merges compiler and runtime errors into the same output panel.

sections.title: Build From Inside the IDE
paragraphs: Build is started by editor_build_project() but executed on a background thread, so the window keeps drawing and the output panel keeps scrolling while packaging runs.

The IDE does not shell out to gcl -build. It calls gcb_build_project_runtime() directly: in the IDE process GCL_EXE_PATH and argv differ from a normal CLI launch, and an external invocation used to fail for that reason. Calling the library function directly removes the whole problem.

The output directory is always the project's own out/ folder. It is created if missing and cleared before writing, so a build never leaves stale artifacts from a previous one. The base executable is copied from GCL_EXE_PATH, renamed to the project name, and finally stamped with the project icon.

code.src:
[Build] 1/3 Packaging project + runtime...
        gcb_build_project_runtime(base_dir, runtime_dir, name, out_dir)
[Build] 2/3 Copying executable...
        copy GCL_EXE_PATH -> <out_dir>/<name>.exe
[Build] 3/3 Done.
        gcl_icon_apply_project(base_dir, dest, name)

notes.text: Each line is appended to project.gclog with its own fopen/fclose. Holding one handle open and never flushing it is exactly why an earlier version left the log empty until the IDE exited.
A build cannot be started twice: while build_running is set the second request only produces the status message "Build already in progress...".

sections.title: The New Project Panel
paragraphs: ide_new_project.c creates a project without invoking gcl -new — the IDE writes the skeleton itself, so it can offer choices the CLI flag set does not express.

GCL is always the core of a project. Lua and Python are independent toggles, and each of them has its own scene template: Empty, 2D or 3D, plus a separate "use raylib" option. Choosing 2D for Python, for example, writes a scripts/main.py that opens a real raylib window with a Camera2D and draws a circle — a starting point that runs immediately instead of an empty file.

sections.title: Settings, Themes and Effects
paragraphs: Settings live in a plain text file, ide.gcsettings, one key=value per line. Its keys map one-to-one onto the GclIdeSettings struct, so reading and writing are symmetric and the file stays human-editable.
There are eight themes: Purple (the default), Black, White, Blue, Orange, Green, Red and Gray. Each theme supplies the full color set listed in the syntax-highlighting table above.

The IDE also has a set of deliberately theatrical visual effects, each with an independent strength slider from 0 to 100: VHS distortion, CRT curvature, screen shake, typewriter sound, pixel particles and text bloom. The screen shake uses an ease-out envelope rather than a linear one, the typewriter sound rises in pitch with each keystroke and fades over time instead of repeating one click, and the particle bursts are pixel-art style squares.

code.src:
font=23
theme=0
syntax_highlight=1
vhs=1
crt=1
screen_shake=1
typewriter=1
particles=1
blink_cursor=1
text_bloom=1
bloom_strength=100
shake_strength=100
particle_strength=100
vhs_strength=100
crt_strength=100
sound=1

notes.text: Defaults are chosen to protect readability: only syntax_highlight and blink_cursor are on by default in code. The heavy effects default to off and to modest strengths, and the bloom only affects text when text_bloom is enabled.
The settings path can be overridden with the GCL_IDE_SETTINGS environment variable — useful for screenshots and automated runs that must not touch the real file.

sections.title: The Settings Panel Is Its Own Module
paragraphs: gcl_settings_panel.c is intentionally self-contained. It keeps its own state — selected tab, scroll offset, open dropdown — inside the module and writes nothing into the Editor struct while it is open.

The reason is a lesson learned the hard way: when UI state was scattered across the shared editor struct, the panel repeatedly came back corrupted after unrelated changes. Keeping the panel's state private gives it a clean lifecycle — open() copies values out of ed.settings into a scratch copy, input() handles ESC and Ctrl+S, draw() renders, and close() either commits or discards.

sections.title: The Output Panel
paragraphs: Program output and build output share one panel backed by a fixed 16 KB character buffer (ed.output) with a length and a scroll offset.

The scroll convention is worth remembering: 0 means "follow" — pinned to the bottom, showing the newest line — and a positive value scrolls upward into history. Long-running programs therefore behave the way people expect without any special-case logic.

rows: A child process is currently alive

sections.title: Verification Hooks
paragraphs: Because a GUI is hard to test from a script, the IDE ships with environment-variable hooks that let an automated run drive it into a specific state and capture it. They are inert unless the variable is set, so normal use is unaffected.

rows: Starts with the split view already enabled, so the split layout and per-pane tab strips can be captured
Programmatically opens the completion popup after a number of frames
Points the settings file at a temporary location

notes.text: The snapshot is taken after about 20 frames on purpose: the placeholder textures, the embedded font and the first layout all have to exist before the picture is meaningful.

sections.title: IDE Source Map
paragraphs: Every file in language/_SRC/ide/ has one job. When something in the IDE misbehaves, this table is the fastest way to find where to look.

sections.title: One Command, Everything Built
paragraphs: The whole toolchain is driven by a single Python script: language/makefile.py. It is invoked either directly (python language/makefile.py) or through the CLI, which simply forwards to it.

Running it with no arguments downloads what is missing, generates the sources that must be generated, then compiles the compiler, the IDE plugin, every native module and both embedded language runtimes. There is no separate configure step and no platform makefile: the script decides everything from platform.system().

code.src:
python language/makefile.py

# or through the CLI:
gcl language

# -> build/<os>/   (windows or gnuLinux)

notes.text: The platform name comes from os_name(): linux is renamed to gnuLinux, everything else keeps its system name. That string is what gcl_os_name() in gcl_os.c returns too, so the CLI and the build agree on the folder name.

sections.title: What the Build Produces
paragraphs: Everything lands under language/build//. This layout is not cosmetic: the interpreter finds native modules by looking in /Library/, the IDE is loaded from /Programs/, and a built game copies this whole tree into its bundle.

code.src:
build/<os>/
    gcl.exe | gcl                # the language: lexer, parser, runner, bundler
    Programs/
        ide.dll | ide.so         # the IDE plugin (loaded by gcl on demand)
    Library/
        Math.dll | Math.so
        Stdio.dll | Stdio.so
        Embed.dll | Embed.so     # Lua + Python runtime + bindings
        Raylib.dll | Raylib.so
        Raygui.dll | Raygui.so
        libraylib.a              # Windows: import lib from Raylib.dll
        Embeded/
            Lua_Runtime/
                lua.dll | lua.so
                LuaRaylib.dll | LuaRaylib.so
                LuaRaygui.dll | LuaRaygui.so
            Python_Runtime/
                Python.dll | Python.so
                libpython3.14.so.1.0     # Linux only
                gcl.so | gcl.pyd         # Python side: import gcl
                raylib.so | raylib.pyd   # Python side: import raylib
                raygui.so | raygui.pyd   # Python side: import raygui
                PyRaylib.dll | PyRaylib.so
                PyRaygui.dll | PyRaygui.so
                Python/                  # Python standard library
    Assets/
        FreeMono.ttf

notes.text: The Linux filename gnuLinux is case-sensitive on purpose. Earlier code used src/IDE on a tree that had _SRC/ide, and the mismatch broke the build on Linux while Windows never noticed.

sections.title: Dependencies Are Fetched Into _temp/<os>/
paragraphs: Nothing is vendored in the repository. Each dependency is downloaded or cloned into _temp// the first time it is needed, and reused afterwards. The per-platform folder means a Windows checkout and a Linux checkout can never mix their binaries.
Each downloader checks first and returns early if the dependency is already present, so a rebuild after a code change does not re-download anything.

rows: Compiled directly into Embed and the Lua runtime modules
The embedded Python runtime and its standard library

notes.text: The Python runtime is downloaded on Linux too, not taken from the system. Previously Linux used the system python3-dev, which sometimes produced a build output with no Python/ directory at all.

sections.title: Platform Correctness in the Dependency Layer
paragraphs: Two details in the dependency layer prevent failures that would otherwise look completely unrelated.

Archive architecture checking. A prebuilt libraylib.a is inspected before it is used: the first member of the archive is extracted and its magic bytes are checked — 64 86 for a Windows COFF AMD64 object, 7F 45 4C 46 (ELF) for a Linux object. If the archive belongs to the other platform it is deleted, along with the stale .o files, and raylib is rebuilt locally. Without this check, a MinGW archive left in the tree would be silently reused on Linux and fail at link time.

Symlink-free extraction. The Python standalone archive contains symlinks, which cannot be created on an NTFS drive mounted from WSL. Extraction therefore filters out symlink and hardlink members instead of aborting with ELOOP. As a follow-up, _ensure_python_so() recreates the missing libpython3.14.so as a real copy of libpython3.14.so.1.0, because the linker needs the unversioned name.

code.src:
ar t libraylib.a          -> first member name
ar p libraylib.a <member>  -> member bytes

Windows : data[0] == 0x64 && data[1] == 0x86   (COFF AMD64)
Linux   : data[:4] == b"\x7fELF"                (ELF)

mismatch -> delete *.a and *.o, rebuild with make/mingw32-make

sections.title: Generated Sources
paragraphs: Three C files used by the build are generated rather than written by hand. All three follow the same idempotency rule: if the generated content is identical to what is already on disk, the file is not rewritten. That matters because rewriting it would change its modification time and force a full recompile of the IDE DLL for nothing.

embed_freemono.c turns FreeMono.ttf into a byte array; embed_icon.c turns assets/icon.png into a byte array that becomes the default icon of every new project; and complete_native_db.c is generated from the module bindings by tools/gen_native_db.py.

notes.text: Because the completion tables are derived from the bindings that are actually compiled, a changed function cannot keep suggesting its old signature — and the generator also cross-checks every binding against the real raylib.h.

sections.title: The Modules — Library/
paragraphs: Every native module implements the same tiny interface from include/gcl_module.h: it exports one function that returns a table of { name, function pointer }. Arguments cross the boundary as strings, and numbers are parsed inside the module with atof.

Math and Stdio are pure C with no external dependency. Embed is the heavy one: it embeds the whole Lua source tree statically, links the Lua raylib and raygui bindings, and — when a Python embed is available — also builds the Python backend.

code.src:
gcc -std=c99 -shared -fPIC -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L \
    -I _SRC/include -I _SRC/embed -I <lua_src> \
    <module sources> \
    -o Library/<Name>.dll|so

rows: Pure C, the {} formatter lives here
Links libraylib.a and the system GL/X11 libraries
Linked against Raylib, never its own raylib

sections.title: The Single-Raylib-Instance Rule
paragraphs: This is the most important linking rule in the project, and getting it wrong produces a very confusing crash: the window simply does not appear, or the program dies on the second frame.

Raygui, LuaRaylib and LuaRaygui all need raylib. If each of them linked its own static libraylib.a, every one would contain its own copy of raylib's global state. The module that called InitWindow would initialize its copy, while a widget calling GuiButton would read a second, uninitialised copy — and raylib is not designed for that.

The fix on Windows is to build an import library: gendef dumps the exports of Raylib.dll into a .def file, and dlltool turns that into libraylib.a. Every consumer then links against that import library, so they all resolve to the one raylib instance inside Raylib.dll.

code.src:
gendef - Raylib.dll                  > Library/raylib.def
dlltool -d Library/raylib.def \
        -l Library/libraylib.a -D Raylib.dll

notes.text: On Linux the static archive is used instead. That is intentional and does not cause the same problem there, because the modules are loaded into a single process and the raylib symbols resolve to one definition.

sections.title: gcl.exe — the Language Only
paragraphs: gcl.exe contains the GCL language and nothing else: the lexer, the parser, the runner, the module loader and the gcBundle reader/packer. It is deliberately kept small — around 660 KB with the icon resource — because it is copied as the base executable of every built game.

The Lua, Python and raylib runtimes were removed from it entirely. gcl -luarun and gcl -pyrun load Library/Embed.dll dynamically and call gcl_lua_run_file / gcl_py_run_file from it. That also means -luarun will not work if the Library/ directory is missing — which is exactly why a bundle always embeds it.

code.src:
gcc -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra ... -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L \
    -I _SRC/ide -I _SRC/build -I _SRC/SharedPipeline \
    -I _SRC/GCL/SimpleRunner -I _SRC/Modules -I _SRC/include -I _SRC/embed \
    <GCL_SRCS> -lm \
    -o build/<os>/gcl[.exe]

notes.text: If _SRC/build/gcbundle_reader.c is missing — for example in a partial CI checkout — the script adds -DGCL_SKIP_BUNDLE, which compiles the bundle code out of gcl_main.c instead of failing the build.

sections.title: ide.dll — the Plugin
paragraphs: The IDE is compiled as a shared library and linked against raylib, the whole completion engine, and the bundle sources — because the IDE performs builds itself. Compiler warnings are deliberately relaxed for it (-Wno-unused-parameter, -Wno-unused-function, and similar) since it consumes a great deal of third-party header code.

The build verifies that the IDE sources actually exist before attempting it. If any are missing it prints exactly which files are absent and skips Programs/ rather than emitting a broken plugin — the CLI then reports clearly that the IDE is unavailable.

sections.title: Linux — Why libpython Is Preloaded
paragraphs: On Linux, Embed.so and the Python-side modules carry a DT_NEEDED entry for libpython3.14.so.1.0. The dynamic linker resolves those entries when the library is opened.

Changing LD_LIBRARY_PATH from inside the program does not help, because the linker has already started. gcl_main.c therefore resolves its own directory, then opens the Python library explicitly with dlopen(..., RTLD_GLOBAL) before any module is loaded. By the time Embed.so is opened, the dependency is already mapped. The same preload is repeated in native_load() in the runner, so a locally run script behaves identically.

notes.text: Without this, the failure message is the misleading unknown module 'Embed' — the module is found, but its dependency cannot be resolved.

sections.title: Building a Project — gcl -build
paragraphs: gcl -build turns a project folder into a runnable, self-contained program. It accepts either the project directory or the project.gcdata file itself, which is worth knowing because passing a directory to a naive reader would fail.

The project root is the parent of project.gcdata. If no -o is given, the output goes to the project's own out/ folder — never to the current working directory, which is what an earlier version did, wiping a repository-level build/ directory as a side effect.

code.src:
1. gcdata_path = <arg>/project.gcdata if arg is a directory
2. name        = "project_name" value read out of the JSON
                  -> leading separators trimmed
                  -> space : ? * " < > | replaced with _
3. project_dir = parent of project.gcdata
4. out_dir     = <project_dir>/out   (when -o is absent)
5. gcl_ensure_dir(out_dir)
   gcl_clear_dir_contents(out_dir)   # no stale artifacts
6. runtime_dir = <exe_dir>            # build/<os>/
7. gcb_build_project_runtime(project_dir, runtime_dir, name, out_dir)
8. copy the running gcl executable -> <out_dir>/<name>.exe
9. gcl_icon_apply_project(project_dir, dest, name)

notes.text: The project name is sanitised before it is used as a file name. A name containing a path separator used to create a subpath inside the output directory, and a stray " or : produced an unopenable file.
The runtime directory is derived from the path of the running executable, not from the current directory. That is what lets gcl -build be run from anywhere.

sections.title: The gcBundle Format
paragraphs: A .gcBundle is a single file that contains the project and the runtime. Its layout is deliberately simple — one header, a table of entries, then the file data as one blob.

The structs are declared with a portable packing macro. GCC and Clang use __attribute__((packed)); MSVC does not understand that attribute at all (it is a compile error there) and uses #pragma pack(1) instead. Both produce byte-identical layouts, so a bundle written on Windows reads correctly on Linux, and the offsets in the file are always written with the compiler's own sizeof().

code.src:
[ GcbHeader ]
  magic[4]        "GCBL"
  version u16     1
  flags   u16     0
  name[64]        project name
  entry_count u32
  entry_offset u32   offset of the entry table
  blob_offset  u32   offset of the file data

[ GcbEntryHeader x entry_count ]
  path[512]
  type u32        0 = FILE, 1 = DIR
  offset u32      file data offset
  size u32        file size

[ blob ]            file contents, back to back

notes.text: Every path inside a bundle is stored with /, even when the bundle was produced on Windows. Windows separators are only used while walking the local filesystem.
The format uses 32-bit offsets, so the whole bundle must fit in 4 GB. The packer computes the total size first and refuses with a clear message instead of silently overflowing into corruption.

sections.title: What Goes Into a Bundle — and What Does Not
paragraphs: A first naive implementation embedded the runtime directory as-is and produced a 1.26 GB bundle. After pruning it lands around 176 MB. The pruning is not cosmetic; it decides whether the format is usable at all.

Files are filtered by suffix (case-insensitively on both platforms, so a Windows-produced .LIB is skipped on Linux too), by directory name, and — for the Python standard library — by package name. The package filter has to look past the platform-specific prefix (Lib/ on Windows versus lib/python3.X/ on Linux) and test every path component, so nested test directories such as xml/test are removed as well.

rows: Headers are not needed at run time
Not needed to run a project

notes.text: Robustness rules in the packer: paths longer than GCB_PATH_MAX are skipped with a message, buffer sizes are checked before snprintf so a truncation can never silently stat the wrong path, and recursion is capped at depth 64 to stop a symlink or junction loop.
An unreadable file or an unlistable directory is skipped on both platforms rather than aborting the build. Only a real out-of-memory condition is treated as an error.

sections.title: How a Built Program Runs
paragraphs: The built executable is a copy of gcl.exe renamed to the project name, with a .gcBundle sitting next to it. With no arguments, gcl_main.c checks its own directory for a bundle before falling back to the IDE — that check is what turns the copy into a game.

The bundle is then opened, its files are extracted next to the executable, and main.gcsf is read out of the bundle and executed. This is the same idea as Godot's PCK: the archive contains the runtime and the scripts; on first run they are materialised on disk so native modules and Embed.Run children can find them.

code.src:
1. gcb_open(bundle_path)
2. gcb_extract_all(b, <dir of the bundle>)     # Library/, scripts/, assets/
3. src = gcb_read_path(b, "main.gcsf", &size)
4. copy src into a NUL-terminated buffer        # the blob is NOT terminated
5. set GCL_PROJECT_DIR / GCL_SHARED_FILE
6. gcl_simple_run_source(src, strlen(src), base_dir, 0, NULL)
7. gcl_shared_cleanup(); gcb_close(b)

notes.text: Step 4 is not optional. The lexer reads up to a null terminator; feeding it the raw blob made it read past the end of the file's data into whatever followed, producing an unexpected character lexer error from random bytes.
Programs/ is never part of a bundle — a game does not need the IDE. Only the scripts, the assets and Library/ are packaged.

sections.title: gcbmod — Inspecting a Bundle
paragraphs: The bundle code ships with its own small command-line tool, built from build/gcbundle_cli.c. It is the quickest way to answer "is this bundle correct?" without running the game.

read writes raw bytes to stdout, and on Windows it explicitly switches stdout to binary mode first — text mode would translate \n and treat the 0x1A byte as end-of-file, quietly corrupting any binary content it extracts.

code.src:
gcbmod pack <dir> <name> <out.gcBundle>
gcbmod info <module.gcBundle>
gcbmod read <module.gcBundle> <path>

sections.title: Build and Run Logs
paragraphs: Both the CLI and the IDE write a log next to the project: project.gclog.

The IDE appends each line by opening and closing the file for that single line. It looks wasteful and it is deliberate: holding one handle open without flushing it left the log empty until the IDE exited, which made a failed build impossible to diagnose from the file.

code.src:
=== Build started ===
[Build] 1/3 Packaging project + runtime...
[Build] 2/3 Copying the executable...
Built: <out>/<name>.exe
Icon applied: <name>
[Build] 3/3 Done.

sections.title: Tests in the Build Tree
paragraphs: Two test programs live beside the sources and are compiled the same way as everything else. They exist because both halves of the system have a real interface that can be verified without opening a window.

tests/parser/test_parser.c drives the lexer and parser directly and checks the resulting AST — the same contract the parser/tests chapter of this book describes. tests/complete/test_complete.c drives the completion engine through its public facade gcl_complete_query(), which is possible precisely because the engine has no raylib dependency.

rows: Tokenising and AST construction for the documented language
Context detection, scope building, member resolution, ranking

notes.text: The pane-state helpers used by the IDE's split view are also written to be testable headlessly for the same reason: no drawing code, only state.

sections.title: Build Troubleshooting
paragraphs: A few failure messages are worth recognising, because the underlying cause is rarely what the message suggests.

rows: The Python shared library was not preloaded — check Library/Embeded/Python_Runtime/libpython3.14.so.1.0
The build did not include the IDE sources; the CLI can run scripts but cannot open the IDE
Raylib links but crashes on the first frame
Two raylib instances — the import library (gendef + dlltool) was not created
The main.gcsf blob was not copied into a null-terminated buffer
The unversioned .so was not created from .so.1.0 (WSL/DrvFs cannot create symlinks)
A bundle is far too large
The Python stdlib filter is not matching — the prefix differs between Lib/ and lib/python3.X/

chapters.title: The Platform — Source Map and Overview

sections.title: The Three Layers
paragraphs: GnuchanOS's language and platform work as three layers that know as little about each other as possible. Understanding which layer owns a problem is the fastest way to find where it lives.

The language is gcl.exe: it reads .gcsf, executes it, loads native modules and packages projects. The platform is the runtime that surrounds it — the native modules in Library/, the embedded Lua and Python runtimes, and the shared cross-process state. The tooling is the IDE plugin and the build script, neither of which the language depends on at run time.

rows: Nothing but the C standard library

notes.text: A useful test of this separation: delete Programs/ and gcl still runs scripts. Delete Library/ and it still parses and runs programs that use no #native module.

sections.title: Directory Map
paragraphs: Everything written by a human lives under language/_SRC/. Everything else is generated, downloaded or built.

The underscore prefix on _SRC is not decoration: the folder used to be called src while include statements referred to _SRC/.... Windows ignored the difference, Linux did not, and the build broke only on Linux. All paths now use _SRC/ with matching case.

sections.title: How a Script Runs — End to End
paragraphs: Tracing one command end to end shows how the pieces connect.

code.src:
gcl_main.c
  read_file(app.gcsf)
  base_dir = absolute folder of app.gcsf
  GCL_PROJECT_DIR  = base_dir           (if not already set)
  GCL_SHARED_FILE  = base_dir/gcl_shared.state
  gcl_simple_run_source(src, len, base_dir, argc=1, argv=["name"])

gcl_simple_runner.c
  collect_native / collect_extern / collect_register
  pp_process          -> macro-expanded text
  gcl_lex             -> tokens (point into the expanded text)
  gcl_parse           -> AST
  gcl_run_program
      load every #native module from Library/
      pass 1: register functions, typedefs, enums, structs
      pass 2: run top-level statements
      call main(argc, argv) if it exists
  free AST, tokens, expanded text   (in that reverse order)

gcl_main.c
  gcl_shared_cleanup()

sections.title: How a Project Becomes a Game — End to End
paragraphs: The second trace is the one that produces something you can hand to another person.

code.file: gcl -build MyGame   (or Build in the IDE)
code.src:
read MyGame/project.gcdata
  name        = "project_name"
  project_dir = MyGame/
  out_dir     = MyGame/out/

ensure + clear out_dir

pack:
  walk project_dir            -> main.gcsf, scripts/, assets/, ...
  walk <exe_dir> as "Library" -> Math, Stdio, Embed, Raylib, Raygui,
                                 Embeded/Lua_Runtime, Embeded/Python_Runtime
  filter out .a .lib .o .h .pyc, test/tkinter/pip, __pycache__
  write  header + entry table + blob  ->  MyGame/out/MyGame.gcBundle

copy <exe_dir>/gcl.exe  ->  MyGame/out/MyGame.exe
apply MyGame/assets/icon.png to MyGame.exe

--- later, on another machine ---

MyGame.exe (no arguments)
  no *.gcBundle next to it?  -> open the IDE
  *.gcBundle found           -> run it:
      extract Library/, scripts/, assets/ next to the exe
      read main.gcsf from the bundle
      set GCL_PROJECT_DIR / GCL_SHARED_FILE
      run it like any other script

notes.text: The extracted files are why a built game can still open Lua/Python windows: the child processes are started as gcl -luarun scripts/main.lua, which needs Library/Embed on disk.

sections.title: Where Lua and Python Fit
paragraphs: Lua and Python are not alternative front ends to GCL. They are guest runtimes started from GCL, each in its own process, with raylib exposed to them through C extension modules.

GCL stays the conductor: it starts the guests, shares variables with them through the memory-mapped store, and waits for them to finish. That design keeps the language small and gives each guest its own window, since raylib only supports one window per process.

notes.text: The full worked example is language/examples/demo_pong_lua_vs_python/: one GCL main.gcsf starts both guests, seeds the shared ball state, and waits for both windows to close.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Invariants
paragraphs: The project targets Windows and GNU/Linux only, and a handful of rules are applied uniformly so behaviour does not diverge between them. These matter because breaking one usually produces a bug on exactly one platform.

Paths inside a bundle always use /. When more than one path separator appears in a string, the last one decides the split — preferring a backslash over a later forward slash truncated mixed paths incorrectly, which is why the same mistake appears fixed in several files. Directory creation normalises separators and skips roots that already exist. Bundle contents are filtered case-insensitively, so filtering does not depend on which platform produced the files.

rows: A bundle written on one platform reads on the other
Sources live in _SRC/ with exact case
Linux is case-sensitive; src/IDE vs _SRC/ide broke the build
Two copies of raylib state crash on the second frame
Python shared library preloaded on Linux
Otherwise modules fail with the misleading unknown module error
A build never writes to the working directory
Output goes to /out, so building cannot clobber unrelated folders

sections.title: Source Conventions
paragraphs: Reading the C sources is meant to be part of the learning experience, so the code follows a small set of habits consistently.

Each file begins with a comment stating its single responsibility. Comments explain why, and many of them record the specific bug the line exists to prevent. Section banners divide long files, and the forward declarations at the top of each file act as its table of contents.

rows: Any file can be read on its own
A header comment naming that responsibility
You know where you are within three lines
Comments record the bug a line prevents
A reader can hold one function in their head
Forward declarations as a table of contents
The shape of the file is visible up front
The project is written by its maintainers in both

sections.title: Status — What "Ready" Means Here
paragraphs: The project README draws a line: the distro is not ready, while the language and platform are. That distinction is precise and worth stating in full, because the two halves of the project have very different maturity.

Ready means: GCL parses and executes the documented language; native modules load and call into C; structs survive the boundary into native code; Lua and Python guests start, run, share variables and exit; projects are created, run, packaged into a single bundle and run again from that bundle; and the IDE loads, edits, completes and builds. All of that is implemented in the files this chapter maps.
Not ready refers to the surrounding operating-system distribution — the shell environment, the package set and the desktop that would carry these tools as a supported product.

notes.text: The GCL language chapters and these internals chapters together cover the whole implemented surface: how to write GCL, and how the thing that runs it is built.
To follow the source in the order it executes, read gcl_main.c, then gcl_simple_runner.c, then gcl_lexer.c, gcl_parser.c and finally gcl_runner.c. That is the same route a .gcsf file takes.
